cards.hypothesis: Subject-specific baseline skin conductance influences wearable stress-detection uncertainty via increased sensor noise.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Higher baseline skin conductance raises electrode-skin interface impedance, amplifying motion artifacts in the PPG signal, which increases model prediction uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Baseline skin conductance → Electrode-skin impedance → Motion artifact amplitude → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences are driven by variations in sensor firmware version across devices.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects using older firmware versions will show higher uncertainty regardless of baseline skin conductance.
cards.distinguishing_test: Within a fixed firmware version, test whether baseline skin conductance still predicts uncertainty; a significant effect supports H1, while non-significance supports the rival.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Prior work shows skin conductance explains roughly 10‑15% of variance in PPG noise levels.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher baseline skin conductance will be associated with higher prediction uncertainty after controlling for temperature, movement, and placement tightness.
cards.failure_condition: No statistically significant association between baseline skin conductance and uncertainty after adjusting for the confounders.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed-effects model with uncertainty as outcome, fixed effect of baseline skin conductance, random intercept for subject, and the three control variables; evaluate the skin conductance coefficient.
cards.falsification_test: Experimentally alter baseline skin conductance via iontophoresis (increase or decrease) while holding temperature, movement, and placement constant; if uncertainty does not change in the predicted direction, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Variability in sensor placement tilt angle leads to differential motion artifact and thus uncertainty in stress detection.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Greater tilt angle increases the lever arm for subject motion, producing larger motion artifacts in the PPG waveform and raising model uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Placement tilt angle → Motion artifact magnitude → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences arise from individual differences in baseline heart‑rate variability (HRV) affecting model confidence.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with lower baseline HRV will have higher uncertainty irrespective of sensor tilt angle.
cards.distinguishing_test: Within subjects, systematically vary tilt angle while holding HRV constant; if uncertainty changes with tilt, H2 is supported; if not, the rival is favored.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Experimental studies report <5% change in signal‑to‑noise ratio for tilt angles under 10 degrees.
cards.testable_prediction: Larger placement tilt angle predicts higher prediction uncertainty after adjusting for activity, adhesion quality, and hair density.
cards.failure_condition: No significant effect of tilt angle on uncertainty after controlling for the confounders.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Repeated‑measures linear mixed model with tilt angle as fixed effect, subject as random intercept, and the three control variables; test the tilt coefficient.
cards.falsification_test: Fix the sensor with a rigid mount that eliminates tilt variation across all sessions; if uncertainty no longer varies with tilt (i.e., shows no tilt‑related differences), the mechanism is supported; if uncertainty still shows tilt‑related patterns, H2 is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Individual baseline cortisol levels modulate stress‑response magnitude, leading to heterogeneous model uncertainty.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Higher baseline cortisol attenuates the physiological stress response, producing smaller changes in stress‑sensitive features and thus higher prediction uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Baseline cortisol → Stress‑response magnitude (cortisol AUC) → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty stems from unequal labeling density of high‑stress epochs across subjects during model training.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with fewer high‑stress labels will exhibit higher uncertainty regardless of baseline cortisol.
cards.distinguishing_test: After controlling for label density, test whether baseline cortisol still predicts uncertainty; a significant effect supports H3, while non‑significance supports the rival.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Baseline cortisol accounts for approximately 12% of variance in stress‑induced cortisol responses in prior literature.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher baseline cortisol predicts higher prediction uncertainty, mediated by a smaller stress‑induced cortisol response.
cards.failure_condition: No significant mediation effect of stress‑response magnitude on the relationship between baseline cortisol and uncertainty.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Mediation analysis using bootstrapped indirect effects: baseline cortisol → stress‑response magnitude → prediction uncertainty, with the three covariates included in both paths.
cards.falsification_test: Pharmacologically lower baseline cortisol (e.g., with metyrapone) and measure whether uncertainty decreases as predicted; if uncertainty does not change, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Cutaneous habituation to prolonged wear reduces sensor‑skin impedance, lowering uncertainty over days.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Repeated wear leads to epidermal remodeling and improved electrode contact, decreasing impedance and motion‑artifact noise, which reduces model uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Days since first wear → Skin adaptation index (impedance reduction) → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty declines because the model accumulates more training samples and improves via online learning, not due to skin changes.
cards.rival_prediction: Uncertainty will decrease with the number of labeled samples regardless of how many days the device has been worn.
cards.distinguishing_test: Match subjects on total labeled samples but vary wear duration; if uncertainty still correlates with days worn, H4 is supported; if not, the rival is favored.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Habituation‑related impedance shifts are typically modest (<10% change) in short‑term wear studies.
cards.testable_prediction: More days of wear predict lower prediction uncertainty after controlling for labeled sample count, firmware version, activity variability, and humidity.
cards.failure_condition: No significant association between days worn and uncertainty after adjusting for the confounders.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed model with uncertainty as outcome, fixed effect of days worn, random intercept for subject, and the three control variables; evaluate the days‑worn coefficient.
cards.falsification_test: Apply a thin, inert barrier layer that prevents epidermal changes while keeping the device worn; if uncertainty still declines over days, skin habituation is not the cause, falsifying H4.

cards.hypothesis: Variability in self‑report accuracy of stress labels introduces label noise that inflates prediction uncertainty for some subjects.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Lower concordance between self‑reported stress and physiological gold standard increases noise in the training targets, causing the model to learn less reliable mappings and output higher uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Self‑report accuracy → Label noise variance → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences are driven primarily by differences in raw sensor signal quality across subjects.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with poorer signal quality will have higher uncertainty irrespective of their self‑report accuracy.
cards.distinguishing_test: Restrict analysis to epochs with comparable signal quality (e.g., top quartile SNR); if self‑report accuracy still predicts uncertainty, H5 is supported; if not, the rival is favored.
cards.effect_size_rationale: The magnitude of label‑noise effects has not been quantified in wearable stress‑detection literature; empirical estimation requires concurrent physiological gold‑standard data.
minimum_data_needed: label_noise_variance (residual variance of self‑report vs gold standard)
cards.testable_prediction: Lower self‑report accuracy predicts higher prediction uncertainty after adjusting for task intensity, awareness, and signal quality.
cards.failure_condition: No significant association between self‑report accuracy and uncertainty after controlling for the three confounders.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Multiple regression of uncertainty on self‑report accuracy with task intensity, awareness, and signal quality as covariates; test the accuracy coefficient.
cards.falsification_test: Replace self‑report labels with objective physiological stress markers (e.g., cortisol AUC) for a subset of subjects; if uncertainty differences disappear, label noise was the driver; if uncertainty differences persist, H5 is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Age‑related increases in skin thickness elevate electrode‑skin impedance, leading to higher uncertainty in older users.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Older age is associated with thicker stratum corneum and epidermis, which raises impedance and degrades signal quality, increasing model uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Age → Skin thickness → Electrode‑skin impedance → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty varies with age due to age‑related declines in autonomic responsiveness (e.g., lower HRV), not skin thickness.
cards.rival_prediction: Older subjects will show higher uncertainty because of reduced HRV, regardless of their skin thickness.
cards.distinguishing_test: After controlling for HRV, test whether skin thickness still predicts uncertainty; a significant effect supports H6, while non‑significance supports the rival.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Skin thickness explains roughly 15% of variance in impedance measurements across adult age ranges in dermatology studies.
cards.testable_prediction: Greater age predicts higher uncertainty via increased skin thickness and impedance, after adjusting for fat, hydration, and medication.
cards.failure_condition: No significant mediation pathway from age through skin thickness and impedance to uncertainty.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Sequential mediation analysis: age → skin thickness → impedance → uncertainty, with fat, hydration, and medication as covariates in each stage.
cards.falsification_test: Apply a conductive gel that equalizes impedance across ages; if age differences in uncertainty persist after impedance normalization, the skin‑thickness mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Subject‑specific muscle tremor frequency contributes to motion‑artifact power in the PPG band, raising uncertainty during low‑activity periods.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Higher frequency tremor injects physiological motion into the same bandwidth as the PPG pulse, increasing artifact power and degrading the signal‑to‑noise ratio, which inflates model uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Muscle tremor frequency → Motion‑artifact power in PPG band → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences arise from variations in baseline heart rate affecting PPG amplitude, not tremor.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with lower baseline heart rate will have lower PPG amplitude and thus higher uncertainty irrespective of tremor frequency.
cards.distinguishing_test: After adjusting for baseline HR and overall movement, test whether tremor frequency still predicts uncertainty; a significant effect supports H7, while non‑significance supports the rival.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Tremor‑related artifact contributions are typically <3% of total PPG variance in resting conditions.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher muscle tremor frequency predicts higher prediction uncertainty after controlling for movement amount, placement location, and skin tone.
cards.failure_condition: No significant association between tremor frequency and uncertainty after adjusting for the three confounders.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed model with uncertainty as outcome, fixed effect of tremor frequency, random intercept for subject, and the three control variables; evaluate the tremor coefficient.
cards.falsification_test: Apply a localized vibration‑damping pad over the muscle group driving tremor; if uncertainty does not decrease as predicted, the tremor mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Ambient light intensity interacts with skin pigmentation to alter PPG signal‑to‑noise ratio, producing subject‑level uncertainty differences.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Higher ambient light increases photon flux; greater melanin absorption raises shot noise, lowering the PPG SNR and increasing model uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Ambient light intensity × Skin pigmentation → PPG SNR → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty stems from inter‑subject differences in vascular density (e.g., capillary count) that affect PPG amplitude independently of light or pigment.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with lower vascular density will have higher uncertainty regardless of ambient light or skin pigmentation.
cards.distinguishing_test: After controlling for vascular density, test whether the interaction of light and pigment still predicts SNR and uncertainty; a significant interaction supports H8, while non‑significance supports the rival.
cards.effect_size_rationale: The combined effect of ambient light and melanin on PPG noise has not been systematically quantified in wearable studies; empirical data are required.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher ambient light and higher pigmentation jointly predict lower PPG SNR and higher prediction uncertainty after adjusting for gain, motion, and temperature.
cards.failure_condition: No significant interaction effect of ambient light and skin pigmentation on PPG SNR or uncertainty after controlling for the confounders.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Hierarchical linear model: first predict PPG SNR from ambient light, pigmentation, and their interaction (plus controls); second, predict uncertainty from the resulting SNR (or include SNR as mediator). Test the interaction term in the first stage.
cards.falsification_test: Use a narrow‑band green LED with tightly controlled intensity and a wavelength‑independent PPG algorithm; if uncertainty differences across pigmentation disappear under fixed lighting, the mechanism is supported; if differences persist, H8 is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Lower baroreceptor sensitivity yields blunted heart‑rate‑variability responses to stress, reducing feature discriminability and increasing model uncertainty.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Reduced baroreceptor buffering leads to smaller stress‑induced HRV changes, providing less informative dynamics for the stress‑detection model, which consequently outputs higher uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Baroreceptor sensitivity → Stress‑induced HRV change → Prediction uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences are due to subject‑specific model calibration errors (e.g., mis‑estimated class priors) rather than physiological differences.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with poorly calibrated models will show higher uncertainty irrespective of their baroreceptor sensitivity.
cards.distinguishing_test: Recalibrate each subject's model using Platt scaling on a held‑out set; if uncertainty still correlates with baroreceptor sensitivity after calibration, H9 is supported; if not, the rival is favored.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Baroreceptor sensitivity explains approximately 10‑12% of variance in stress‑induced HRV changes in psychophysiology literature.
cards.testable_prediction: Lower baroreceptor sensitivity predicts higher prediction uncertainty mediated by a smaller stress‑induced HRV response, after adjusting for baseline HRV, medication, and caffeine.
cards.failure_condition: No significant mediation effect of stress‑induced HRV change on the relationship between baroreceptor sensitivity and uncertainty.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Mediation analysis with bootstrapped indirect effects: baroreceptor sensitivity → stress‑induced HRV change → prediction uncertainty, including baseline HRV, medication, and caffeine as covariates in both paths.
cards.falsification_test: Administer a low dose of phenylephrine to transiently increase baroreceptor sensitivity and measure whether uncertainty decreases as predicted; if uncertainty does not change, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Subject‑level heteroscedasticity in model residuals drives apparent uncertainty differences; modeling subject‑specific variance components reduces this variation.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Greater unexplained residual variance for a subject indicates a noisier data‑generating process, which the predictive distribution captures as higher uncertainty.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences arise from shifts in feature means (e.g., average heart rate) across subjects, not from residual variance.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with extreme mean feature values will have higher uncertainty regardless of their residual variance.
cards.distinguishing_test: Fit a heteroscedastic model that estimates subject‑specific variance; if residual variance no longer predicts uncertainty after this modeling, the rival (mean‑shift) is favored; if it still predicts uncertainty, H10 is supported.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Accounting for heteroscedasticity often explains a substantial portion (>30%) of uncertainty variation in similar sensor‑data modeling contexts.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher subject‑specific residual variance predicts higher prediction uncertainty after controlling for model complexity, training set size, and label noise.
cards.failure_condition: No significant association between subject residual variance and uncertainty after adjusting for the three confounders.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear regression of uncertainty on subject residual variance with the three control variables; test the variance coefficient.
cards.falsification_test: Apply a variance‑stabilizing transformation (e.g., log) to the raw sensor features, refit the model forcing homoscedastic residuals, and recompute uncertainty; if subject‑level uncertainty differences persist, heteroscedasticity is not the primary driver, falsifying H10.
